current_episode.title: Talking gibberish and siloed solutions: how water issues can learn from both nature, and Janet and John

guest.bio_context: Matt Wilden is Infrastructure Development Director at Wessex Water, where his work focuses on educating and influencing policy, regulation, economic incentives, and technical guidance related to rainwater management. He is actively working with government on changing regulatory frameworks and will be speaking about policy change at an upcoming event.

context.real_quote: We talk gibberish and then we talk in complicated language. No wonder we're not making progress.

pending_qa.q: What is the fundamental problem with how water companies currently approach infrastructure solutions?
pending_qa.r: Water companies focus on big grey centralized solutions like the Thames Tideway Tunnel and large new reservoirs, but the real problem is how homes are built and how rain is managed. Because rain is not managed where it lands, companies are solving the wrong problem at enormous cost rather than addressing the actual issue of poor rainwater management at the source.

pending_qa.q: What percentage of England's rainfall actually enters the public water supply system?
pending_qa.r: Only 3% of the rain that lands on England goes into the public water supply, meaning 97% of the water cycle is being ignored. Water companies represent only about 3% of the entire water cycle, yet the current system relies entirely on them to collect, treat, and pump water for non-potable purposes like toilet flushing.

pending_qa.q: How much energy is required to pump drinking water to an average home, and what is the carbon cost?
pending_qa.r: The average pumping head is about 100 metres, and with 138 litres per head per day usage, this is equivalent to lifting a kilogram of sugar twice the height of Everest per person per day. This ginormous energy requirement and carbon cost is not being discussed when water companies promote net zero homes that still require massive energy inputs for water delivery.

pending_qa.q: What regulatory and economic barriers prevent water companies from implementing source control and decentralized rainwater solutions?
pending_qa.r: Water companies face legal barriers without explicit powers, but more significantly, they are disincentivized because decentralized solutions are classified as OPEX rather than CAPEX. Additionally, regulatory certainty targets like storm overflow reduction drive companies toward low-risk, concrete-based storage solutions rather than nature-based source control approaches.

pending_qa.q: What can the average property owner capture from rainwater landing on their roof annually?
pending_qa.r: Enough rain lands on the average roof to supply all of your non-potable demands all year if you had the right infrastructure to capture it and use it. Despite living in a country that is not dry on average, poor storage and collection infrastructure across multiple locations means this natural resource is not being utilized.

pending_qa.q: Which countries are ahead of the United Kingdom in implementing rainwater management and incentive policies?
pending_qa.r: Germany and Belgium have implemented policy that incentivizes societal responsibility for the rain that lands on property, and Australia has been in crisis mode for years due to climate pressures. These nations are making decisions now about infrastructure that will make them far more climate resilient than the UK unless the UK changes course.

pending_qa.q: What is the core message that water companies should communicate to change public perception and drive policy reform?
pending_qa.r: The core narrative must be simple: 'Manage rain better where it lands, harness nature, mimic nature.' This simple message focuses on emotion and avoids technical jargon. Once this common narrative is established, legislation, regulation, economic incentives, technical guidance, and education will follow, enabling systemic change across all other areas.
